mcqs.question: A team merges small changes into main several times a day but only runs their test suite manually, right before a release. Are they practicing CI?
options: No — CI requires both frequent merges and automatic verification on every merge, and they're missing the second half
Yes — merging often is the only requirement for CI
Yes, as long as the test suite eventually runs before the code ships
No — CI requires long-lived feature branches to be meaningful
mcqs.explanation: CI is two commitments together: merging often AND verifying automatically on every merge. Running tests manually before a release recreates the pre-CI pattern of discovering problems late, just with smaller batches — the automatic, per-merge verification is exactly what's missing.

mcqs.question: Why do CI practitioners push slow end-to-end and performance suites out of the merge-blocking pipeline rather than just letting the pipeline take 45 minutes?
options: End-to-end tests are less reliable than unit tests, so they shouldn't run at all
CI servers cannot execute tests that take longer than 10 minutes
A slow required pipeline erodes CI's core value — fast feedback — and developers start batching changes to avoid running it, which recreates integration hell
Performance tests only produce meaningful results when run on a schedule
mcqs.explanation: CI's benefit is proportional to how quickly it reports a problem. A slow required pipeline makes developers avoid running it constantly, undermining the whole practice — so the fix is tiering (fast checks block merge, slow ones run after), not accepting the slowness or discarding the tests.

mcqs.question: What problem does marking a CI check as "required" under branch protection solve that code review alone does not?
options: It makes the test suite run faster
It replaces the need for a human reviewer entirely
It automatically fixes failing tests before merge
It removes reliance on a reviewer correctly assuming tests passed — the platform blocks the merge mechanically until CI reports green
mcqs.explanation: A required check is enforced by the platform, not by a reviewer's judgment — so a reviewer approving code without re-verifying every detail is safe, because the merge is mechanically blocked until the check passes. It doesn't speed up tests or remove the need for review.

mcqs.question: A team puts its full end-to-end browser suite into the required, merge-blocking CI check alongside unit tests. What's the most likely consequence, and what's the better structure?
options: No consequence — more tests in the blocking path always means a safer main branch
The pipeline duration climbs and developers start avoiding frequent merges; better to tier tests so fast unit/integration tests block merge and slow e2e suites run after merge
The e2e suite should be removed from CI entirely and only run manually before releases
Unit tests should be moved out of the blocking path instead, since they add the least value
mcqs.explanation: Piling every test into the blocking path drives pipeline time up and erodes fast feedback, pushing teams back toward batching. The fix is a test pyramid: fast tests block merge, slow ones still run — just after merge or on a schedule — rather than dropping them or gating on the wrong layer.

mcqs.question: A flaky test starts failing intermittently, and engineers begin merging past it anyway, assuming "it's probably not my change." What's the real risk in letting this continue?
options: The team gradually stops trusting or acting on CI failures, so a genuine regression can hide inside the tolerated red and reach production unnoticed
The pipeline will eventually run out of compute resources
Flaky tests automatically get skipped by most CI systems, so there's no real risk
It only slows down the pipeline, with no effect on release quality
mcqs.explanation: Tolerating red status trains the team to ignore CI signal altogether — the pipeline keeps running, but nobody believes it, so a real failure can hide among the accepted noise. It's a trust problem, not just a performance or resource one.
